statusDetail: Coverage-complete model audit across five representative public templates/journeys. The requested Spanish host redirects most inspected paths to English; this is reported as a finding rather than an execution blocker.

findings.summary: The Spanish hostname redirects visitors to the English site and declares English document language.
findings.evidence: The recon probe requested es.scribd.com but ended at https://www.scribd.com/, with html lang="en-US" and English title/content. The category and signup probes likewise ended on English pages; signup explicitly passed ui_locales=en.
findings.suggestedFix: Preserve the Spanish locale through redirects and auth handoffs, render translated content, set lang="es", and keep localized canonical/hreflang signals aligned.

findings.summary: A consent wall obscures the content on every fresh entry, especially on mobile.
findings.evidence: Desktop, mobile, category, and search screenshots show a fixed consent panel covering most or all of the first viewport before any user interaction. Mobile users see no page content behind the full-height panel.
findings.suggestedFix: Use a compact, non-blocking consent surface with essential-only defaults and an equally prominent reject action; keep core content usable before a choice.

findings.summary: The experience does not adapt to the user’s dark color-scheme preference.
findings.evidence: The dark-emulated screenshot is pixel-identical in palette to the light capture, and the computed platform probe reports colorScheme="normal".
findings.suggestedFix: Declare color-scheme and use prefers-color-scheme or light-dark() tokens for surfaces, text, controls, and the consent UI.

findings.summary: The throttled mobile load is slow and main-thread heavy.
findings.evidence: Lighthouse measured LCP 18.5 s, TBT 715 ms, Speed Index 7.8 s, and performance score 0.40. An unthrottled trace was much faster (LCP 1.48 s), showing the weakness is condition-sensitive rather than universal.
findings.suggestedFix: Profile the throttled LCP chain, prioritize the hero/LCP resource, delay non-critical third-party work, and split or defer long JavaScript tasks.

findings.summary: The entry page ships a large amount of unused JavaScript and non-critical third-party code.
findings.evidence: HAR recorded 2.85 MB across 73 requests, including 2.13 MB of JavaScript. Lighthouse estimated 909 KiB unused JavaScript, including Stripe, Survicate, multiple Google tags, Facebook, and application chunks.
findings.suggestedFix: Load payment, survey, advertising, and analytics code only after intent/consent; consolidate tags and route-split application bundles.

findings.summary: Several interactive targets are too small for reliable touch use.
findings.evidence: The platform probe found 16x16 consent checkboxes, many 15–23 px-high links, and 1 px skip/back-to-top controls. Lighthouse automated accessibility otherwise scored 1.0.
findings.suggestedFix: Expand interactive hit areas to at least 24x24 CSS px (prefer 44x44 for primary touch controls) without shrinking visible focus indicators.

findings.summary: Core listing content is effectively unavailable without JavaScript.
findings.evidence: The category discoverability capture reported isJsShell=true and only 2% content overlap; title and h1 were absent from raw HTML. The homepage had only 10% overlap, while the document page retained 23%.
findings.suggestedFix: Server-render category headings, document links, and essential descriptions as semantic HTML, then hydrate enhancements progressively.

findings.summary: Non-JavaScript crawlers receive almost none of the category’s meaningful content.
findings.evidence: The discoverability primitive found 2% rendered-word coverage, classified the category as a JS shell, and found neither title nor h1 in raw HTML. Browser/crawler screenshot pairs visibly diverge.
findings.suggestedFix: Render category content and real document hrefs in the HTTP response; retain canonical, hreflang, title, and description in crawler-visible markup.

findings.summary: Important browser security policies are missing and first-party identifiers use permissive cookie settings.
findings.evidence: Headers capture found no CSP, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options/frame-ancestors, Referrer-Policy, or Permissions-Policy; HSTS was present. Two 400-day identifier cookies use SameSite=None and are not HttpOnly.
findings.suggestedFix: Deploy an enforceable CSP, nosniff, clickjacking defense, Referrer-Policy, and least-privilege Permissions-Policy; tighten identifier cookie scope, lifetime, and SameSite.

findings.summary: The initial page has an unusually broad tracking and third-party footprint.
findings.evidence: Tracker capture found 17 third-party origins and known Google Analytics/Ads, Facebook, Sentry, and Tag Manager trackers. HAR attributed 70 of 73 requests and almost all 2.85 MB to origins other than es.scribd.com. No sensitive client secret was detected.
findings.suggestedFix: Apply data minimisation, gate optional trackers behind consent, remove duplicate analytics/ad tags, shorten retention, and proxy or self-host essential assets where appropriate.

findings.summary: The consent interface preselects targeted advertising, personalization, storage, and performance cookies.
findings.evidence: Initial screenshots show all four optional-looking purposes checked, alongside text covering 53 IAB partners, precise geolocation, and device-characteristic scanning. Reject is available but requires action after the biased defaults are presented.
findings.suggestedFix: Default optional purposes off, separate essential processing from advertising, explain each purpose plainly, and make accept/reject/save equally clear and persistent.

findings.summary: Third-party scripts dominate the page’s transfer and execution budget.
findings.evidence: HAR measured 2.85 MB total with 2.13 MB scripts and 2.85 MB attributed to non-es.scribd.com origins; large items include multiple Google tags, Stripe, Facebook, Survicate, and consent tooling before user intent.
findings.suggestedFix: Set a third-party byte/request budget, load integrations on demand, remove duplicate tags, and defer background analytics until idle and consented.

findings.summary: Some links use generic text that does not describe their destination.
findings.evidence: Lighthouse SEO identified two “Learn more” links pointing to copyright FAQs, reducing context for crawlers and assistive navigation.
findings.suggestedFix: Use destination-specific link text such as “Learn about Scribd copyright handling”.

findings.summary: The consent modal uses custom role-based containers rather than the native dialog primitive.
findings.evidence: The platform probe found 0 dialog elements and 2 role=dialog containers; screenshots show a custom fixed modal surface.
findings.suggestedFix: Use a native dialog for the modal consent flow with explicit focus management and predictable close behavior, while keeping rejection available.

findings.summary: Document discovery has no structured agent capability and major AI crawlers are explicitly blocked.
findings.evidence: The platform probe found no manifest/tool surface, and robots.txt disallows ClaudeBot, Claude-Web, CCBot, Bytespider, and others. Document raw HTML preserves some metadata but only 23% rendered-word coverage.
findings.suggestedFix: If agent access is intentional, expose narrowly scoped read/search tools with clear authorization and safety boundaries, and align robots policy with that intent.

taskList.title: Restore a real Spanish-localized journey across content and auth
Replace biased full-screen consent with essential-only, non-blocking consent
Cut unused and third-party JavaScript from the critical load
Server-render category and document discovery content
Deploy missing browser security policies and tighten cookies
Increase touch target hit areas and improve generic link text
Use a semantic dialog for the consent modal
Define and expose a safe agent-access policy if desired
